\chapter{Short Replies}
\label{ch:ta-replies}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer with five short replies in Tamil, from a flat agreement to a hedge.}

Complete TA-C47-just-so and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[uṇmai]{\ta{உண்மை} (uṇmai) — the truth}

\label{lesson:TA-C47-true}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{vivasāyi} mean, and what did \emph{viruntāḷi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{உண்மை}}
\textbf{\ta{உண்மை}} (\emph{uṇmai}) — \textquotedblleft{}the truth\textquotedblright{}.

It is built out of \emph{uḷ}, 'to be, to exist', and the \emph{-mai} Tamil adds to turn a quality into something you can name. The truth, then, is is-ness: what is the case.

As a reply it stands on its own. Somebody tells you something surprising and \emph{uṇmai} means \textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{uṇmaiyā?}, with the question fixed to the end, means \textquotedblleft{}really?\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five short replies.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uṇmai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{uṇmai}, then \emph{sari}, so the two agreements sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{உண்மை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the truth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pōdum]{\ta{போதும்} (pōdum) — that is enough}

\label{lesson:TA-C47-enough}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{uṇmai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{போதும்}}
\textbf{\ta{போதும்}} (\emph{pōdum}) — \textquotedblleft{}that is enough\textquotedblright{}.

It grows out of \emph{pōdu}, 'to suffice', and it is the polite full stop of a Tamil meal: your host is serving, your plate is filling, and \emph{pōdum} stops it without giving offence. Said twice — \emph{pōdum pōdum} — it means you are serious.

It has nothing to do with \emph{pō}, 'to go', though the two look alike at a glance. Different roots, similar clothes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: agreeing, and calling a halt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pōdum}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{uṇmai}, then \emph{pōdum}, and let the second land firmly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{போதும்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}that is enough\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[niccayamāka]{\ta{நிச்சயமாக} (niccayamāka) — certainly}

\label{lesson:TA-C47-certainly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pōdum} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நிச்சயமாக}}
\textbf{\ta{நிச்சயமாக}} (\emph{niccayamāka}) — \textquotedblleft{}certainly\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{niścaya}, 'a settled thing', plus \emph{-āka}, the ending Tamil adds when a word is to describe how something is done. \emph{niccayam} on its own is the certainty; \emph{niccayamāka} is doing the thing certainly.

That same \emph{-āka} is inside \emph{nalamāka}, from the answer about being well, so the shape is already in your ear.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the third leaves no room for doubt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{niccayamāka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pōdum}, then \emph{niccayamāka}, and feel how much longer the second is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நிச்சயமாக} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}certainly\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[oruvēḷai]{\ta{ஒருவேளை} (oruvēḷai) — perhaps}

\label{lesson:TA-C47-perhaps}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{niccayamāka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஒருவேளை}}
\textbf{\ta{ஒருவேளை}} (\emph{oruvēḷai}) — \textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{}.

Two pieces welded together: \emph{oru}, 'one', which you have, and \emph{vēḷai}, 'an occasion, a time', which you have not. One occasion out of the several that could happen — which is exactly the claim \textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{} makes.

Tamil builds its hedge out of counting. English does the same trick with \textquotedblleft{}maybe\textquotedblright{}, which is a \textquotedblleft{}may\textquotedblright{} and a \textquotedblleft{}be\textquotedblright{} pushed against each other until they stuck.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth one steps back from the other three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{oruvēḷai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{niccayamāka}, then \emph{oruvēḷai}, and hear the certainty drain out
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{ஒருவேளை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[appaḍiyē]{\ta{அப்படியே} (appaḍiyē) — just so}

\label{lesson:TA-C47-just-so}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{oruvēḷai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அப்படியே}}
\textbf{\ta{அப்படியே}} (\emph{appaḍiyē}) — \textquotedblleft{}just so\textquotedblright{}.

The front of it is the far pointer \emph{a-} from \emph{adu} and \emph{aṅgē}; \emph{appaḍi} is 'in that manner'; and the \emph{-ē} on the end is how Tamil presses down on a word. In that manner, precisely.

Move the pointer and the whole set follows: \emph{ippaḍi}, 'like this', and \emph{eppaḍi}, 'how' — which you have been saying since you first asked somebody how they were. One pattern, three words, and only the front letter moves.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: true, enough, certainly, perhaps, just so.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{appaḍiyē}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{uṇmai}, \emph{pōdum}, \emph{niccayamāka}, \emph{oruvēḷai}, \emph{appaḍiyē}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{அப்படியே} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}just so\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
